# From Technology- Challenged Teachers to Empowered Digitalized Citizens: Exploring the Profiles and Antecedents of Teacher AI Literacy in the Chinese EFL Context

Ziwen Pan[1](#from-technology--challenged-teachers-to-empowered-digitalized-citizens-exploring-the-profiles-and-antecedents-of-teacher-ai-literacy-in-the-chinese-efl-context)[ ](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6018-4129)\| Yongliang Wang[2](mailto:)

1Department of English, Chinese University of Hongkong, Hongkong, People's Republic of China \| 2School of Foreign Studies, North China University of Water Resources and Electric Power, Zhengzhou, People's Republic of China

**Correspondence:** Yongliang Wang ([wangyongliang@ncwu.edu.cn)](mailto:wangyongliang@ncwu.edu.cn) **Received:** 1 October 2024 \| **Revised:** 13 January 2025 \| **Accepted:** 15 January 2025

**Funding:** The study reported in this paper represents a contribution to “Model Construction and Application of Artificial Intelligence Empowered Language Education in the Era of Digital Intelligence” (grant no. 202410012) funded by Start- Up Research Project for newly recruited PhD holders, and also funded by “Research- based class construction and teaching practice among postgraduate students in Humanities and Social Sciences” at North China University of Water Resources and Electric Power, China.

**Keywords:** Chinese EFL context \| latent profile analysis \| mixed- methodology \| teacher AI literacy

## ABSTRACT Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy has come to the spotlight, empowering individuals to adeptly navigate the modern digitalised world. However, studies on teacher AI literacy in the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) context remain limited. This study aims to identify intraindividual differences in AI literacy and examine its associations with age and years of teaching experience among 782 English teachers. Given the absence of a reliable instrument to measure teacher AI literacy, we first constructed and validated a scale encompassing five sub- scales: _AI Knowledge_, _AI Use_, _AI Assessment_, _AI Design_, and _AI Ethics_. Subsequently, latent profile analysis (LPA) was conducted using _Mplus_ 7.4, with the results revealing four distinct profiles: Poor AI literacy (C1: 12.1%), Moderate AI literacy (C2: 45.5%), Good AI literacy (C3: 28.4%), and Excellent AI literacy (C4: 14.1%). Multinomial logistic regression analyses indicated significant associations between teacher AI literacy and both age and years of teaching experience. Additionally, 32 respondents participated in semi- structured interviews. The qualitative data analysed with MAXQDA 2022 tri- angulated the quantitative results and offered deeper insights into teachers’ perceptions of their AI literacy. This study provides both theoretical and practical implications for understanding teacher AI literacy in the Chinese EFL context.

[https://doi.org/10.1111/ejed.70020](https://doi.org/10.1111/ejed.70020) fundamental changes, alongside the burgeoning of AI, have also introduced new demands for teachers' competencies. Beyond their traditional role as knowledge transmitters, teachers are now expected to guide students to become digital citizens, en- abling them to navigate and thrive in the digital society (Endris et al. 2024).

While the role of AI in macro and L2 education has been rec- ognised, many teachers still struggle to grasp the underlying concepts of AI and effectively design AI- empowered curricula (Ng et al. 2021). Besides, concerns regarding data leakage, ac- ademic honesty, and algorithmic bias persist (Rudolph, Tan, and Tan  2023). These issues collectively give rise to the term “teacher AI literacy,” which encompasses a set of competen- cies enabling teachers to critically understand, evaluate, and design AI technologies to address real- life problems (Long and Magerko 2020). The AI competency framework for teachers re- leased by UNESCO (2024) highlights teacher AI literacy as es- sential for empowering teachers to live, learn, and work with AI- driven technologies in the digitalised 21st century. From a pluralistic and sociocultural view, teacher AI literacy is of more significance as it equips educators to nurture students into re- sponsible digital citizens, better preparing them for the unprece- dented challenges of this era (Liu, Darvin, and Ma 2024).

Given the pivotal role of teacher AI literacy in the contempo- rary era, it is essential to direct more research toward this area. However, prior research on AI literacy has primarily focused on general education, neglecting the unique context of Chinese L2 education (Ding et al. 2024; Kim and Kwon 2023; Wang 2017; Wu and Pan 2024). Besides, much of the existing research has focused on K- 16 classrooms aimed at developing students' AI lit- eracy (Ng et al. 2022; Sperling et al. 2024), with little attention to teachers' AI literacy. Furthermore, to the best of our knowledge, no reliable scale is currently available for quantitatively assess- ing teachers' AI literacy to data. Inspired by these gaps, we set out to unveil the intricate profiles of Chinese EFL teachers' AI literacy. Our study employed a mixed- methods approach with a sequential explanatory design. The quantitative analysis fo- cused on identifying profiles of AI literacy, while the qualitative analysis explored the antecedents associated with these profiles. By shedding light on EFL teachers' AI literacy, our study prom- ises to initiate a new inquiry into teachers' AI literacy in the Chinese EFL context.

**2 \| Literature Review**

**2.1 \| Conceptualisations of AI Literacy**

The definition of literacy varies, but it generally refers to the capacity to identify, comprehend, interpret, and cre- ate through printed and written materials in different con- texts (UNESCO  2024). In the fast- changing world marked by technological advancements, the concept of literacy has broadened, giving rise to new forms of literacy such as media literacy, information literacy, computer literacy, and AI literacy (Chan  2024; Fernández- Otoya et al. 2024; Kähler, Hahn, and Köller  2024; Wang, Gao, and Wang, 2024; Wang, Gao, Wang, et  al.  2024; Wang, Wu, et  al.  2024; Wang, Sun, et  al.  2023; Wang, Wang, et  al.  2023). As AI continues to permeate and 

revolutionise our lives (Huang, Wang, and Zhang 2024; Wang and Reynolds 2024), it has become increasingly important for individuals to develop literacy related to AI, which enables them to understand and effectively use AI- based technologies (Gao, Wang, and Wang  2024; Wang, Gao, and Wang,  2024; Wang, Gao, Wang, et al. 2024; Wang, Wu, et al. 2024; Wang and Xue 2024). In this sense, AI literacy, a fusion of AI and literacy, comes to the spotlight. The term “AI literacy” was first intro- duced by Burgsteiner, Kandlhofer, and Steinbauer (2016), who characterised it as the ability to grasp the underlying knowledge of AI technologies. Long and Magerko  (2020) expanded this definition, suggesting that AI literacy encompasses a range of competencies that empower people to communicate and collab- orate with AI in a critical, ethical, and effective manner. Based on their definition, it is essential to recognise that AI literacy has extended beyond traditional digital literacy. In the educa- tional context, AI literacy primarily branches into two areas: student AI literacy and teacher AI literacy. The former centres on students' perceived abilities, motivation, and confidence to cultivate a comprehensive understanding of AI across affective, behavioural and cognitive dimensions (O'Dea et al. 2024; Wu, Wang, and Wang 2024). The latter, in contrast, examines how teachers nurture AI awareness in themselves and students by creating and developing AI curricula, learning applications, and educational models (Ng et al. 2022; Sperling et al. 2024; Wang, Wu et al. 2024). In the present study, AI literacy is specifically characterised as teacher AI literacy, emphasising teachers' en- deavours to equip students with essential literacy skills for an AI- saturated future and their own capabilities to live, learn, and work through AI- driven technologies in the digitalised world.

**2.2 \| The AI Literacy Theoretical Model**

Given the role of AI literacy in shaping educational practices, it is essential to anchor this exploration within a solid theoret- ical framework (Younis 2024). In this study, we have adopted Bloom's (1956) taxonomy as our theoretical rationale, as its hier- archical structure of cognitive skills—ranging from knowing to creating—offers a systematic lens to examine the development of AI literacy among EFL teachers (Adams [2015)](#author-contributions-ziwen-pan-conceptualisation-methodology-data-curation-writing--visualisation-investigation-software-validation-writing--reviewing-and-editing-formal-analysis-yongliang-wang-conceptualisation-meth--odology-data-collection-writing--original-draft-preparation-validation-writing--reviewing-and-editing-formal-analysis-funding-acquisition-project-administration-and-supervision). Specifically, the knowing stage involves acquiring foundational knowledge about AI, such as key concepts (e.g., machine learning, natural language processing) and their potential applications in lan- guage education. The understanding stage builds on this by en- abling teachers to explain the functionalities of specific AI tools and how these tools can be aligned with pedagogical objectives. Moving to applying, teachers can integrate AI tools into class- room practice, such as using AI- powered grammar checkers or language apps to personalise learning. At the analysing stage, teachers critically evaluate the effectiveness, biases, and limita- tions of AI tools, identifying their impact on student outcomes. The evaluating stage requires teachers to assess the ethical and pedagogical implications of AI, ensuring that its use aligns with teaching goals and addresses concerns such as data privacy or algorithmic bias. Finally, in the creating stage, teachers are ca- pable of designing innovative, AI- enhanced teaching strategies and materials that foster interactive and adaptive learning ex- periences. Each stage of cognitive development within Bloom's framework can align with the progression of AI literacy acqui- sition in language teaching contexts. Moreover, considering AI 

literacy is a relatively new concept with limited research on its cognitive process dimensions (Ayanwale et  al.  2024), Bloom's Taxonomy fits in this gap and offers valuable insights into the cognitive patterns and developmental stages of AI literacy among EFL teachers.

Despite the acknowledged benefits, Bloom's Taxonomy, orig- inally designed to categorise cognitive skills, may not fully capture the nuanced demands of AI literacy (Ng et al. 2022). AI literacy is a multifaceted concept that extends beyond cog- nitive understanding to include practical, technical, and ethical competencies (Su 2024; Zhao, Wu, and Luo 2022). Recognising these limitations, Ng et al. (2021) built upon Bloom's Taxonomy to propose a more comprehensive framework, encompassing four key aspects: (1) know and understand AI, (2) use and apply AI, (3) evaluate and create AI, and (4) AI ethics (see Figure 1). This framework not only integrates cognitive skills but also addresses the ethical implications of AI use in educational set- tings, an increasingly critical component of AI literacy (Ng et al. 2022). To integrate the framework with AI literacy, the first as- pect, _know and understand AI_, involves acquiring foundational knowledge about AI. This stage equips teachers with the theo- retical grounding necessary to comprehend how AI functions and how it can potentially enhance language learning. Without this foundational knowledge, teachers may struggle to make informed decisions about selecting or implementing AI tools in their classrooms. The second aspect, _use and apply AI_, em- phasises the practical integration of AI tools into teaching prac- tices. This involves leveraging AI- driven applications, such as automated grading systems, adaptive learning platforms, and AI- based language practice tools, to enhance instructional ef- fectiveness and personalise learning. The third aspect, _evaluate and create AI_, focuses on higher- order cognitive and creative skills. Teachers must be able to critically assess the strengths and limitations of AI tools, evaluating their pedagogical value, accuracy, and potential biases. Additionally, this aspect involves fostering creativity by enabling teachers to design or adapt AI- enhanced teaching materials and methodologies tailored to their students' unique needs. Finally, _AI ethics_ addresses the ethical considerations surrounding the use of AI in education. 

**FIGURE 1** \| AI literacy and Bloom's taxonomy.

This includes understanding the implications of data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the potential for AI to reinforce existing inequalities. Teachers need to ensure that AI tools are used re- sponsibly and equitably, fostering a classroom environment that prioritises fairness and transparency. Ng et al.'s framework thus evidently offers a more comprehensive approach to AI literacy by not only encompassing the cognitive dimensions outlined in Bloom's Taxonomy but also addressing the practical, creative, and ethical competencies essential for AI literacy in educational contexts. Moreover, Ng et al. (2022) emphasised that prior stud- ies on AI literacy often focus disproportionately on lower- order cognitive skills, such as remembering and understanding, while neglecting higher- order skills like designing and assessing. Given that some teachers are already leveraging their prior ex- perience to create original artefacts and make informed deci- sions using AI applications in both professional and personal contexts (Hur 2024), it becomes evident that a robust framework is needed—one that captures the full spectrum of AI literacy competencies. In light of these considerations, we have adopted Ng et al.'s (2021) framework as the primary theoretical rationale for our study. Compared to Bloom's Taxonomy, Ng et al.'s model offers a more nuanced and holistic understanding of AI liter- acy by integrating cognitive, practical, and ethical dimensions (Elim 2024) (see Figure 2). This comprehensive approach aligns well with our study's focus on examining the multifaceted na- ture of AI literacy among EFL teachers, providing a robust foun- dation for our research.

**2.3 \| Related Studies on AI Literacy**

While AI literacy remains an emerging issue (Yao and Wang 2024), it has garnered significant attention due to its po- tential to prepare individuals to thrive in a technology- driven world. A thorough review of literature in macro education re- veals that existing studies on AI literacy encompass the entire K- 16 spectrum, from early childhood to tertiary education, yielding positive outcomes (Kong et al. 2024; Su 2024). For ex- ample, many studies focusing on higher education indicated that teachers were inclined to use project- based or hands- on

experiential learning to introduce AI concepts to students (Wang and Xue  2024; Wang, Sun, et  al.  2023; Wang, Wang, et  al.  2023; Zhi, Wang, and Wang  2024). While these studies have made significant contributions to advancing AI literacy in general education, they primarily focus on students' AI literacy. In contrast, research dedicated to the AI literacy of teachers is limited (Sperling et al. 2024), despite their recognition as one of the key stakeholders in the educational context (Derakhshan et al. 2022). Furthermore, most investigations into AI literacy emphasise a single dimension, such as the understanding or practical application of AI (Ng et al. 2022), neglecting a compre- hensive approach that cultivates both individuals' cognitive and practical AI- related abilities.

In EFL education, one significant aspect of AI literacy concern- ing the use of AI technologies has been explored (Hur 2024; Yetişensoy 2024; Yildirim, Camci, and Aygar 2023). For ex- ample, to examine the role of Pigai in enhancing students' ac- ademic writing skills, Wu, Wu, and Zhang (2021) conducted a study that utilised both quantitative data from 1952 under- graduates and qualitative insights from 15 respondents. The results indicated that Pigai could significantly improve stu- dents' English academic writing abilities by providing person- alised feedback and identifying both surface- level and deeper errors such as clarity and logical flow. Additionally, another line of research has shifted focus to the emotional and mental states of language learners, exploring how AI- driven second language education influences students' motivation (Zheng et al. 2024), engagement (Dai and Wang 2024), willingness to communicate (Guo, Wang, and Ortega Martín 2023; Zhi and Wang  2024), and emotional regulation strategies (Yang and Zhao 2024). Despite these extensive investigations, a thorough review of literature reveals a significant gap in grasping the status quo of AI literacy among foreign language teachers (Ng et al. 2022). One possible explanation for this is the absence of a reliable scale tailored to the Chinese EFL context for measur- ing teachers' AI literacy (Zhao, Wu, and Luo 2022). Without a standardised scale, it becomes challenging to systematically and comprehensively assess the multifaceted nature of teach- ers' AI literacy. Moreover, a well- designed scale could facil- itate large- scale data collection, making it easier to identify patterns and profiles of AI literacy among teachers—insights that may be less readily captured through qualitative meth- ods alone. Furthermore, as Yao and Wang (2024) pointed out, extant research on AI literacy lacks rigorous experimental de- signs, with most studies being review studies rather than em- pirical investigations. Studies that combine both quantitative 

and qualitative methods remain scarce (Fernández- Otoya et al. 2024). To sum up, the gaps mentioned above collectively underscore an urgent need to unveil the intricacies of Chinese EFL teacher AI literacy under a robust and rigorous design. A key step in addressing these gaps is the development of a reli- able and valid scale tailored to the Chinese EFL context. Such a tool is essential for systematically assessing the multifaceted nature of teacher AI literacy, identifying distinct profiles, and uncovering the underlying factors that influence these compe- tencies. Given that the extant research on AI literacy of EFL teachers is still in its infancy (Yao and Wang 2024), examining its profiles and antecedents through a well- designed scale can significantly contribute to advancing this field of investiga- tion. In response to these identified gaps, our current study aimed to address the following three questions:

RQ1. _What components constitute the teacher AI literacy scale, and how reliable and valid is it in assessing teacher AI literacy in the Chinese EFL context?_

RQ2. _What are the profiles of Chinese EFL teachers' AI literacy?_

RQ3. _What are the antecedents of Chinese EFL teachers' AI literacy?_

**3 \| Research Methods**

**3.1 \| Instruments**

In the present study, a self- designed scale was utilised to assess the AI literacy of Chinese EFL teachers. The final validated scale included 31 items with five subscales: AI Knowledge (7 items), AI Use (8 items), AI Assessment (5 items), AI Design (5 items), and AI Ethics (7 items). The dimensions of this scale were developed based on Ng et al.'s (2021, 2022) theoretical framework, which comprehensively addresses AI literacy by incorporating cognitive, practical, and ethical competen- cies. Specifically, the AI Knowledge subscale was designed to measure teachers' understanding of fundamental AI con- cepts, drawing upon prior research that emphasises the im- portance of foundational knowledge in fostering AI literacy (Ng et  al.  2022). The AI Use subscale focused on practical skills, reflecting the ability to integrate AI tools into teaching practices, as highlighted in studies on technology- enhanced education (Wang and Xue  2024). AI Assessment captured teachers' ability to critically evaluate the effectiveness, biases, 

and limitations of AI tools. The AI Design subscale assessed teachers' capacity to create or adapt AI- driven instructional materials, a competency that has been linked to innovative pedagogical practices (Hur 2024). Finally, the AI Ethics sub- scale was grounded in the growing recognition of the ethical considerations surrounding AI use in education, such as data privacy and algorithmic bias (Ng et al.  2022). To ensure the relevance of the questions and to minimise potential misun- derstandings and any vagueness, two experts in applied lin- guistics carefully reviewed all items and gave constructive feedback. Participants responded to each item on a 5- point Likert scale from 1 (_strongly disagree_) to 5 (_strongly agree_). Responses with higher scores indicate greater teacher AI liter- acy. The reliability index of the scale estimated via Cronbach's alpha was 0.84, which indicated a high level of reliability.

ranging from 25 to 58 years. In terms of teaching experience, most participants had been teaching for 5 to 8 years, with an average of 5.3 years, suggesting that they were in a relatively mature stage of their professional careers. Of the 782 respon- dents, the majority held PhD degrees (_N_ = 597), while 126 held master's degrees, and 32 held bachelor's degrees. Participants were teaching different courses in their profession, including English Literature (352), English Linguistics (259), English Translation (97), and Business English (74). The participants for the quantitative analysis were divided into two groups: the first group, consisting of 377 participants, provided data for the Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA). The second group, comprising 405 participants, contributed to both the EFA and profile analysis. Detailed demographic information is pre- sented below (Table 1).

For the qualitative interviews, 32 EFL teachers (male = 12, fe- male = 20) who had previously completed the questionnaire were selected to participate in this interview. The participants' ages ranged from 28 to 47 years, with an average teaching expe- rience of 5.4 years. Regarding ethical considerations, the study received approval from the ethics committees of The Chinese University of Hong Kong and North China University of Water Resources and Electric Power.

**3.3 \| Data Collection**

Data collection was conducted in two stages, spanning from May 2024 to June 2024. In the first stage, after addressing any potential issues with the scale, we distributed it to university teachers through Wenjuanxing, a popular APP to collect data in China. After 3 weeks, we collected a total of 832 responses. In the second stage, 32 respondents were selected from the pool of participants who had indicated their willingness to participate in follow- up interviews. The selection process was informed by the quantitative results, ensuring a diverse repre- sentation of teachers across different AI literacy profiles (i.e., Poor, Moderate, Good, and Excellent). **3.4 \| Data Analysis**

The analysis was conducted in three phases using SPSS 26.0, Mplus 7.4, and MAXQDA 2022 based on the research ques- tions. In the initial stage, we carefully inspected any prob- lematic cases in the collected dataset. The thorough data screening left a total of 782 cleaned cases after eliminating 24 cases with decreasing patterns, 18 with increasing patterns, and 8 with a finishing time of less than 60 s. Afterwards, to answer RQ1, we adopted an EFA to test the factor structure of the scale in hopes of specifying the underlying dimensions of teachers' AI literacy. To this end, principal axis factoring anal- ysis with oblique rotation (oblimin) was utilised. Cronbach's alpha reliability coefficients were also calculated to ensure the reliability of the scale.

For RQ2, a latent profile analysis (LPA) was conducted to un- cover distinct patterns of teacher AI literacy, following the ap- proach outlined by Bergman and Andersson  (2010). Models were tested to determine the optimal number of classes and identify the best- fitting solution. To evaluate model fit, we calcu- lated three key information criteria: the Akaike information cri- terion (AIC) (Akaike 1973), the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) (Schwarz 1978), and the sample- size adjusted BIC (ABIC) (Sclove  1987). In addition, we used the Lo–Mendell–Rubin likelihood ratio test (LMR) (Lo 2001) and the bootstrap likeli- hood ratio test (BLRT) (McLachlan and Peel 2000) to compare

models. Both tests provided _p_- values to determine whether a simpler model with fewer profiles should be rejected in favour of a more complex one. We also examined entropy values, which reflect classification accuracy; higher entropy values (closer to 1) indicate better differentiation between profiles. Based on these statistical indicators, we selected the number and composition of profiles that offered the best fit and interpretability. Finally, multinomial logistic regression was conducted to explore the associations between teachers' AI literacy profiles and demo- graphic factors, such as age and years of teaching experience.

To answer RQ3, MAXQDA 2022 was used to analyse the col- lected qualitative data, which consisted of 17,236 English words. We adopted Braun and Clarke's (2006) six- step thematic analy- sis approach. First, we familiarised ourselves with the data by thoroughly reading and re- reading the participants' responses, ensuring a deep understanding of the dataset. Next, we gener- ated initial codes by systematically coding the entire dataset. In the third step, we searched for themes, where similar codes were grouped together to identify recurring concepts and ideas. To ensure inner validity and reliability, the first author and the corresponding author coded the texts independently and then compared their processed codes to identify any contradictions or disagreements, followed by further discussions refining the cod- ing system to enhance its accuracy and consistency. The last two steps involved defining themes and reporting the results with illustrative quotes to support key findings. We also compared the qualitative results with the quantitative findings to achieve triangulation, ensuring a more comprehensive understanding of the data. This is how the qualitative analysis was conducted.

**4 \| Results**

**4.1 \| Construct Validity and Reliability**

After data cleansing and screening, 426 cases were obtained for further analysis. EFA was adopted to identify the underlying pattern of teachers' AI literacy. The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO)

measure of sampling adequacy indicated a satisfactory value of 0.836. Additionally, Bartlett's test was significant (_p_ \< 0.01), confirming that the variables were interrelated and suitable for EFA. Given the sample size in our study, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was used as the extraction method to uncover the underlying structure of the data. Furthermore, since the initial inspection revealed significant correlations among the variables, we employed the Promax rotation method to allow for correlated factors. Table 2 shows the total variance explained by these factors.

According to Table  2, the EFA with PCA resulted in the ex- traction of five factors with eigenvalues above 1, jointly explain- ing 60.4% of the variance in teachers' AI literacy.

Based on the rotated pattern matrix results, items loaded below 

0.3 were suppressed as they did not contribute significantly to the factors. Six items (Q7, Q14, Q16, Q21, Q24, Q27) were ex- cluded because they could not load onto any factor. In total, 34 items were retained for further analysis as they demonstrated substantial loadings on the identified factors. Through an in- depth analysis of their content and comparison with existing literature (Ng et al. 2022; Zhao, Wu, and Luo 2022), we have named these factors as follows: Factor 1: _Teachers' AI knowledge_ (8 items), Factor 2: _Teachers' AI use_ (8 items), Factor 3: _Teachers' AI assessment_ (5 items), Factor 4: _Teachers' AI design_ (6 items), and Factor 5: _Teachers' AI ethics_ (7 items).

After this, the revised scale with 34 items was distributed to the second group (_N_ = 405) for further validation. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted to test the fit of the pro- posed factor structure derived from the EFA. According to the standardised and unstandardized estimates, all items demon- strated significant loadings on their respective constructs, except for three items (Q6, Q 11, and Q26) with standardised loadings below 0.5, which, according to Kline  (2016), could jeopardise the model's convergent validity. compared to those aged over 41, EFL teachers whose age ranges from 27 to 31 and 32 to 36 had a higher probability of belonging to the moderate AI literacy profile than the poor AI literacy pro- file, and those with their age from 37 to 41 had a higher probabil- ity of belonging to the excellent AI literacy profile.

Years of teaching experience also shows a strong association with AI literacy profile membership. Compared to those with more than 12 years of teaching experience, an increase of one unit in teaching experience for those with 8–11 years of experi- ence corresponded to an increase in the likelihood of 6.341 times for the Moderate AI Literacy profile. In addition, an increase of one unit in years of teaching experience for those who have been teaching for 0–3 years corresponded to an increase in the likeli- hood of 5.775 times for the Good AI Literacy profile. For those with 4–7 years of teaching experience, the probability of being classified into the Excellent AI Literacy profile is 6.259 times that of being classified into the Poor AI Literacy profile.

**4.4 \| Analysis of the Antecedents**

Regarding the contributing factors for teacher AI literacy, as re- vealed in Figure 2, two themes were identified: positive factors (97 references) and negative factors (31 references). Positive fac- tors explain why teachers achieve excellent, good, or moderate levels of AI literacy, while negative factors illustrate the chal- lenges that may hinder a high level of AI literacy or lead to poor levels of AI literacy. The total number of references for positive factors (97 references) significantly exceeds that of negative fac- tors (31 references), suggesting that teachers generally perceive more enablers than barriers in developing their AI literacy. This contrast highlights a promising outlook: while challenges exist, the factors that facilitate teachers' AI literacy appear more prevalent and impactful. To provide greater clarity, this section distinguishes between primary (which exert a foundational influence) and secondary factors (which have a conditional or supplementary impact) within each category based on their fre- quency and centrality to AI literacy.

**4.4.1** \| **Positive Factors**

Among the positive factors, the support system (54 references) was identified as the primary factor due to its essential role in driving AI literacy. It consists of two subcategories: self- driving forces (29 references) and external support (25 references). Self- driving forces, such as commitment to modernising teaching (16 references), personal interest (8 references), and profes- sional growth (5 references), serve as intrinsic motivators that consistently propel teachers toward improving their AI literacy. External support, including training sessions (12 references), in- stitutional resources (8 references), and peer assistance (5 refer- ences), provides critical enablers that sustain and enhance these internal motivations. Together, these elements form the founda- tion of teachers' ability to develop AI literacy.

Teacher 2 (42- year- old male with 18 years of teaching expe- rience; the sub- theme: training sessions): Through attending lectures and training, I have come to realise the importance of mastering AI- related technology.

Teacher 7 (36- year- old male with 9 years of teaching experience; the sub- theme: personal interest): I have always been deeply in- terested in the use of computer technology in teaching and have applied it in my own teaching practice.

Teacher 14 (41- year- old female with 14 years of teaching experi- ence; the sub- theme: professional growth): No matter who you are, to be a professional teacher, enhancing AI literacy is an es- sential requirement.

By contrast, powerful functions (43 references) were classified as a secondary factor, as their influence depends on teachers' awareness and perception of AI's benefits. This factor includes three subcategories: effectiveness in language teaching (22 references), reducing workload (12 references), and enhanc- ing academic performance (9 references). While teachers who recognised these benefits were motivated to improve their AI literacy, the impact of this factor varied across individuals and was less consistent compared to the primary factor support system.

Teacher 11 (29- year- old male with 2 years of teaching experi- ence; the sub- theme: reducing workload): I often use GPT to handle tasks outside of work, which helps to alleviate my work- load pressure.

Teacher 23 (34- year- old female with 5 years of teaching expe- rience; the sub- theme: effectiveness in language teaching): AI software can assist me in grading student essays, paying atten- tion to language issues and improving efficiency.

**4.4.2** \| **Negative Factors**

Within the negative factors, AI- related deficiencies (21 refer- ences) were deemed the primary obstacle due to their direct and systemic nature. These deficiencies included data privacy concerns (7 references), unsatisfactory AI- generated outputs (5 references), limited access to AI tools (4 references), high costs (3 references), and ethical concerns (2 references). Such issues con- sistently prevented teachers from fully integrating AI into their teaching practices, making them the most significant barriers to AI literacy. These underlying factors are best illustrated in the following excerpts:

Teacher 7 (55- year- old female with 23 years of teaching experi- ence; the sub- theme: limited access to AI tools): The availability of AI technology is an important factor. For example, getting the latest version of ChatGPT from abroad could come with some cost issues.

Teacher 18 (39- year- old male with 11 years of teaching expe- rience; the sub- theme: unsatisfactory AI- generated outputs): Compared to teachers, AI lacks emotional resonance and cannot fully grasp the complex emotions and needs of students.

On the other hand, teacher- related issues (10 references) were classified as a secondary factor, as their impact was more indi- vidualised. Some teachers openly acknowledged in the inter- view that certain personal factors also contributed to their lower levels of AI literacy (see comments from Teacher 16 and Teacher 

27). They identified antecedents such as the degrading learning capability (5 references), fixed teaching mindsets (3 references), and little time and energy (2 references) as key reasons for this. In other words, as their learning capacity declined and their teaching methods became more ingrained, it became increas- ingly difficult to keep up with AI advancements. Additionally, the demands of their daily responsibilities left them with little time and energy to invest in learning and using AI, thereby lim- iting their ability to improve their AI literacy. Figure 4 presents the specific codes.

Teacher 16 (55- year- old female with 18 years of teaching experi- ence; the sub- theme: degrading learning ability): I don't have a strong desire to embrace, learn, and use new skills.

Teacher 27 (46- year- old female with 15 years of teaching ex- perience; the sub- theme: little time and energy): Learning AI technology requires a significant investment of time and energy, and after a long day at work, I simply don't have that much time to spare.

**5 \| Discussion**

This study endeavoured to contribute to the investigation of teacher AI literacy by examining its profiles and antecedents within the Chinese EFL context. To do so, three research ques- tions were formed based on identified gaps in existing research. The study employed a mixed- methods approach to address these three questions, providing an in- depth view of teacher AI liter- acy in the Chinese EFL context.

Regarding the first research question, the findings indi- cated that the self- designed scale is valid, consisting of five sub- scales: AI knowledge (7 items), AI use (8 items), AI de- sign (5 items), AI assessment (5 items), and AI ethics (6 items). While the scale comprises five dimensions, it aligns 

**FIGURE 4** \| Antecedents for different levels of AI literacy.

conceptually with the six cognitive domains of Bloom's Taxonomy (Bloom  1956) by addressing a progressive hier- archy of competencies. Such a successive alignment further supports a systematic review by Ng et al. (2022), who high- lighted the urgent need to encompass more fundamental ca- pabilities in AI literacy, such as decomposing AI problems or building AI applications. Besides, each component of the scale addresses distinct yet interrelated competencies essential for AI, collectively providing a comprehensive view of AI literacy. Specifically, AI knowledge is conceptualised as the mastery of essential concepts and an understanding of AI tools and tech- nologies (Yildirim and Atasoy  2023). This definition aligns with Burgsteiner, Kandlhofer, and Steinbauer (2016) charac- terisation of AI literacy as the ability to comprehend different techniques in various AI- driven products and accessible ser- vices. AI use, on the other hand, emphasises the ability to use AI- related applications in the educational context or in indi- viduals' everyday lives (Wang and Xue 2024). This definition is in line with Wu, Wang, and Wang's (2024) emphasis on the role of teachers' ability to use AI tools in supporting students' understanding of AI mechanisms. The third component, AI Design, resonates with Ng et al. (2022), who argued that indi- viduals should critically learn how to create AI technologies and collaborate effectively with AI. AI Assessment addresses the role of critical evaluation in using AI, consistent with Long and Magerko (2020), who defined AI literacy as the abil- ity to critically evaluate AI technologies. The last component, AI ethics, stays in tune with AI learning modules proposed by Zhang et al. (2023), where the importance of adhering to eth- ical principles when engaging with AI technologies is empha- sised. By addressing competencies ranging from foundational knowledge to ethical considerations, the scale offers a holistic tool for evaluating and enhancing teachers' AI literacy. This comprehensive approach ensures that the scale is not only the- oretically grounded but also practically applicable in diverse educational contexts, contributing significantly to the grow- ing body of research in AI literacy.

11 of 16

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

In terms of the second question, we adopted LPA and iden- tified four profiles of teacher AI literacy: poor AI literacy (12.1%), moderate AI literacy (45.4%), good AI literacy (28.4%), and excellent AI literacy (14.2%). Notably, the majority of Chinese EFL teachers rated their AI literacy as moderate or above, accounting for 87.9% of respondents, while only a small percentage (12.1%) considered their AI literacy to be poor. This finding aligns with the AI competency report released by UNESCO (2024), which suggests that China has made sig- nificant progress in integrating AI education into workforce development. Despite this, it is too premature to embrace full optimism, as a closer look at these profiles revealed that most teachers still perceived their AI literacy to be at a moderate or good level (73.8%), with only a small proportion rating it as excellent (14.1%). This suggests substantial room for im- provement. Besides, decent attention should also be paid to teachers who perceive their AI literacy as poor, underscoring the need for targeted support to enhance their AI literacy (Fan and Zhang 2024).

Given that teacher AI literacy is still in its infancy and that rele- vant literature is limited (Ayanwale et al. 2024; Kong et al. 2024), identifying the underlying reasons for the differences in these profiles presents a challenge. However, despite the intricacies, we can still glean some insights into sub- factors by examining each profile more closely. It could be found that AI Knowledge, AI Use, and AI Ethics consistently occupy relatively higher proportions within each profile, while AI Assessment and AI Design tend to be lower across all profiles. This finding is con- sistent with Ng et al.'s (2022) review study, which indicates that teachers prioritise understanding specific concepts of AI and utilising AI technologies while often struggling with the critical evaluation and design of AI systems. One plausible explanation for this discrepancy is that most EFL teachers come from English major backgrounds, which may result in limited training related to programming and computational concepts, making it chal- lenging to engage effectively in evaluating and designing AI sys- tems. Moreover, as Ding (2024) reported in her qualitative study, the overwhelming workload suffered by Chinese EFL teachers may inhibit their enthusiasm to design AI tools.

To further unveil the nuanced intricacy of teacher AI literacy, we also examined the association between two demographic characteristics (age and years of teaching experience) and teacher AI literacy. In terms of age, taking the poor AI literacy profile as a reference category, we found that most respondents who rated their AI literacy as moderate were aged between 27 and 36, while those who classified themselves in the excellent AI literacy profile were predominantly between 37 and 41 years old. Such a discrepancy further highlights the age effects in teachers' cognitive and practical competency in the field of macro edu- cation (Dubravac, Roebers, and Meier 2022; Seibt et al. 2015). Furthermore, this finding aligns with Sun et al.'s (2024) qual- itative study, which highlighted that those pre- service teachers encountered challenges in being ready for AI, ranging from comprehending AI knowledge to integrating AI tools into their classrooms. Regarding potential reasons for this discrepancy, existing literature has revealed that early- career teachers with less teaching experience generally have less AI readiness to en- gage with new educational technologies, whereas older teachers tend to possess a wealth of relevant experience that enhances 

their ability to integrate AI into their instructional practice (Ghiasvand, Kogani, and Alipoor 2024).

It should also be noted that as age increases with years of teach- ing experience, these two demographic characteristics exhibit similar patterns in their association with teacher AI literacy. Early- career teachers (0–3 years) are more likely to be classi- fied in the Good AI Literacy profile, likely due to their recent exposure to AI during pre- service training and their openness to exploring new tools without being constrained by established routines. In contrast, mid- career teachers (4–7 years) exhibit the highest likelihood of belonging to the Excellent AI literacy profile. This group benefits from an optimal balance between pedagogical confidence and a willingness to innovate, allowing them to integrate AI tools effectively into their teaching prac- tices. Teachers with 8–11 years of experience tend to fall within the moderate AI literacy profile, as they may rely more on tradi- tional teaching methods while gradually incorporating AI tools. Their extensive teaching experience provides a solid foundation, but their pace of adoption may be slower compared to less ex- perienced colleagues. Finally, highly experienced teachers (12+ years) show comparatively lower AI literacy, potentially due to resistance to change, limited exposure to AI during their initial training, or a preference for familiar teaching practices. These findings underscore the dynamic relationship between teaching experience and AI literacy, highlighting the need for differenti- ated professional development strategies that cater to the unique strengths and challenges of teachers at various career stages.

For the third research question, which aims to explore the an- tecedents of teacher AI literacy, the results revealed both posi- tive and negative factors contributing to explaining variations in literacy levels. Interviewees predominantly identified sup- port systems and AI's powerful functions as key antecedents of their AI literacy. This result echoes Wang, Sun, et al. (2023) and Wang, Wang, et al. (2023) urge that institutions should provide enhanced support and resources to foster teachers' professional development. Conversely, AI- related and teacher- related an- tecedents were perceived as key barriers to achieving AI literacy. Such a finding stays in tune with the result of Su's (2024) study, indicating that teachers' engagement at work could predict their readiness to use AI. Furthermore, the extensive qualitative data regarding the nuanced perceptions of teacher AI literacy further corroborates Ng et al.'s (2022) claim that future research on AI literacy should be enriched through more qualitative methods such as interviews and reflective blogs.

**6 \| Conclusions and Future Enquiries**

Through the lens of Bloom's Taxonomy, we explored the profiles and antecedents of Chinese EFL teachers' AI literacy. Due to the absence of a reliable and valid scale for measuring teacher AI literacy, we first validated a scale that identifies five com- ponents through an EFA. The CFA results then validated this scale, demonstrating its high reliability and validity for measur- ing EFL teacher AI literacy. Following this, we conducted LPA using Mplus 7.4 to identify four distinct profiles of teacher AI literacy: poor AI literacy, moderate AI literacy, good AI liter- acy, and excellent AI literacy. We also examined the association between two demographic factors (age and years of teaching 

experience) and teacher AI literacy. We also conducted quali- tative interviews with 32 teachers to gain deeper insights into their nuanced perceptions of AI literacy.

The present study holds both theoretical and practical impli- cations. Theoretically, by drawing on insights from Bloom's Taxonomy, this study not only enriches its framework but also reinforces its explanatory power within the Chinese EFL con- text. Practically, this study provides a comprehensive overview of teacher AI literacy by identifying distinct profiles (poor, moderate, good, and excellent), thereby offering a more nu- anced understanding of AI literacy among Chinese teachers. Additionally, the development of a context- specific scale tai- lored to measure AI literacy in the Chinese EFL context marks a significant contribution to ongoing research in this field. Our quantitative and qualitative findings also have key implica- tions for Chinese EFL teachers, teacher trainers, educational institutions, and policymakers. The profiles and the association between AI literacy and demographic characteristics (age and years of teaching experience) can offer actionable insights for tailoring teacher training programs and institutional support. Specifically, for teachers in the poor AI literacy profile, typically younger and with less teaching experience, foundational train- ing should focus on building basic AI knowledge and confidence in using simple AI tools, such as grammar checkers or language learning apps. Structured guidance and mentoring from ex- perienced teachers may help these individuals overcome their initial barriers to AI integration. Teachers in the moderate AI literacy profile, often in their late 20s to mid- 30s, could bene- fit from targeted workshops that deepen their understanding of AI's pedagogical applications, such as using AI- driven platforms for personalised student feedback and classroom management. For the good AI literacy profile, which encompasses more expe- rienced teachers, advanced professional development programs should focus on enhancing their ability to critically evaluate AI tools and design AI- integrated instructional strategies, ensur- ing that these tools align with their pedagogical goals. Finally, teachers in the excellent AI literacy profile, who typically have extensive teaching experience, are well- positioned to serve as AI literacy leaders. These individuals could take on mentoring roles, guiding less experienced colleagues in effectively inte- grating AI and fostering a culture of technological innovation within their institutions. Educational institutions and policy- makers must also consider the role of demographic factors in shaping AI literacy. Our findings suggest that older teachers with more teaching experience tend to possess higher AI lit- eracy, likely due to their ability to draw on past experiences in adopting new technologies. Thus, teacher training programs should adopt differentiated approaches that cater to varying lev- els of AI literacy, ensuring that both early- career and veteran teachers receive tailored support. Institutions can foster AI lit- eracy by providing sustained professional development oppor- tunities, organising collaborative learning sessions, and offering accessible online training resources. Moreover, the qualitative findings of this study underscore the importance of institutional support, as many teachers attributed their AI literacy develop- ment to resources and encouragement provided by their schools. Finally, given that the exploration of teacher AI literacy is still in its infancy, it is crucial for policymakers to establish a system- atic framework for evaluating and promoting AI literacy among teachers. This framework should be tailored to the unique needs 

of the Chinese educational context and aim to deepen the theo- retical foundations of AI literacy while guiding practical imple- mentations in schools and classrooms.

Despite the contributions, our study is subject to several limita- tions. Firstly, we did not consider the potential impact of demo- graphic factors on the variables when developing the scale, which may hamper the reliability of the scale. Future research could consider the mediating role of such factors. Second, the AI assess- ment subscale in our instrument demonstrated a relatively low internal consistency coefficient (_α_ = 0.570), indicating a need for refinement. While this does not invalidate the findings, the low α value suggests weaker correlations among items, potentially af- fecting the reliability of the results. This further highlights the importance of revising item formulations or conducting further validation to enhance the scale's consistency. Besides, this study utilised a cross- sectional design, failing to examine temporal changes in teacher AI literacy. To address this limitation, future research could adopt a longitudinal approach, allowing for a more nuanced analysis that incorporates temporal factors when examining profiles (Lei, Wen, and Yang 2023). Furthermore, the limited literature on the factors influencing teacher AI literacy means that some of our interpretations of the profiles are based on broader assumptions or hypotheses. This suggests more em- pirical studies are needed to incorporate teacher AI literacy as a variable and explore specific antecedents that may influence or mediate it within the EFL context. Last, our analysis did not ac- count for contextual or cultural factors when examining the pro- files, which may introduce bias into the findings. Future research could consider these elements to gain a deeper understanding of how culture influences teacher AI literacy.
